newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South African asset managers favour bonds for '97.
newsitem.headline: South African asset managers favour bonds for '97.

text.p: South African asset managers favour cash or bonds for the next quarter, while opinions on equity prospects are mixed.
BOE Asset Management managing director John Winship told Reuters that in the short term he would continue to exploit high returns on cash.
"The general view right now is to prefer liquidity. Our lightened (third quarter) bond exposure reflected concern about interest rates, which has been proved correct.
"When you get 16 or 16.5 percent in cash, well, why not? We'll continue to enjoy our liquidity for a while yet - it's certainly paying off handsomely," he said.
Syfrets portfolio manager Denzil Newman, however, said his firm had shifted from cash to bonds and would keep it that way.

"Our thinking is that in the short to medium end we expect better returns from bonds than from cash. We're still heavy in bonds - 17 to 20 percent in most of our funds - and we are still anticipating good value," he said.
Adrian Allardice, senior portfolio manager at Old Mutual, indicated a shift in strategy in the new year after a strong move into equities in the third quarter of 1996.
"I think next year could be very good for cash and bonds. I would not be at all surprised if next year the bond market does very well," he said.
"We moved our equity weightings up in the third quarter...we went from the low sixties to the high sixties, but that was not a view on the market, it was a view on particular shares."
Allardice said bargains were becoming harder to find amongst rand hedge stocks and no sector looked compellingly cheap, prompting him to look for short-term opportunities in bonds.

The latest quarterly survey of pension fund asset distribution by First Bowring insurance brokers reflects an overall increase in funds' equity weightings from 63.6 percent on June 30 to 64.2 percent at the end of the third quarter.
The survey covers institutions with full discretionary control over some 140 billion rand in South African pension fund investments.

Property holdings fell over from 5.8 percent of total pension fund investments to 4.8 percent, largely as a result of the government's decision to tax the net rental income of pension funds at 17 percent.

Fixed-interest securities increased from 19.9 percent to 21.4 percent and cash holdings dropped from 10.1 percent to nine percent, but this was the overall outcome of contradictory movements reported by individual asset managers.

Old Mutual's "Profile" range of pension fund products moved sharply out of bonds during the third quarter, but in a shift not matched at the same level by any other fund, tended towards equities rather than cash or property.

In direct contrast, Investec's executive director for investments Brett Comley confirmed that he had moved from equities into bonds and cash in the third quarter. He raised the fixed-interest exposure of his investment funds from 17.2 percent to 25.3 ercent and the cash exposure of his managed funds to from 5.8 to 12.8 percent.
Comley said the move was in anticipation of the sort of volatility that emerged in the wake of U.S. federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's recent warning of over-valuation.

"Personally, I think its the right time to start looking at equities again. If we get the macro-economic factors in place - union acceptance of the growth, employment and redistribution strategy (GEAR), movement on privatisation, less volatility in th rand - then we could see very good 1998/99 rates in growth stocks," he said.

Acceptance and implementation of GEAR, Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's strategy to boost employment and double economic growth to six percent by the turn of the century, was cited by most investors as a key factor in the performance of the South Afrian economy next year.
The Board of Executors shifted the distribution of its pension fund holdings of almost 10 billion rand significantly from bonds into cash, raising the cash weighting to around 20 percent.
-- Cape Town newsroom 27 21 252238
